clue.text: Force in uniform, wearing female garb?

indicators.note: something worn goes inside the clothes, so one piece sits within the garment

blocks.note: U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a dress is a garment traditionally worn by women

explanation.surface: A police force in uniform, oddly dressed in women's clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force in uniform' reads as a body of officers; in fact 'Force' is the definition and 'in' belongs to the container instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Duress means compulsion or pressure applied to make someone act against their will.

clue.text: Broadcast doubts over wicket with large dry area

indicators.note: to broadcast is to scatter seed widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
W is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for wicket
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator voices doubts about a pitch that has become large and parched.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' suggests radio commentary on a cricket pitch, but it tells you to scatter the letters of the following words together.
explanation.definitionFit: A dust bowl is a region stripped of soil by drought and wind, as on the American plains in the 1930s.

clue.text: Phone dodgy seller set aside

blocks.note: to ring someone is to phone them
a fence is a person who sells stolen goods

explanation.surface: Someone phones a shady salesman who has put something aside for them.
explanation.walkthrough: A fence is slang for a receiver and seller of stolen property; the surface makes 'dodgy seller' sound like the person being phoned.
explanation.definitionFit: To ring-fence money is to reserve it for one purpose so it cannot be spent elsewhere.

clue.text: Highly noted surgeon’s op ran overtime somewhat

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only a portion of the run of letters is used

blocks.note: the letters run across the apostrophe-s, the second word, the third and the start of the fourth

explanation.surface: A well-known surgeon's operation overran its schedule a little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Highly noted' looks like praise for the surgeon; it is a playful definition of a singer whose notes are high.
explanation.definitionFit: A soprano sings in the highest vocal range, so her notes are pitched high.

clue.text: Do LSD lab cooking? That’s nuts

indicators.note: cooking transforms raw ingredients, so the letters are mixed into something new

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone proposes brewing drugs in a laboratory and is told the idea is crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooking' is also slang for making drugs, which suits the lab scene. Here 'nuts' is a plural noun meaning eccentric people, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuts, as a noun, are crazy or eccentric people, the same as oddballs.

clue.text: Regret meeting with detectives

blocks.note: DI is detective inspector, so two or more are DIs
an appointment is an arranged meeting

explanation.surface: Someone is sorry to have had a meeting with the police.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are joined in the reverse of the clue order: 'with' lets the detectives come first.
explanation.definitionFit: Disappointment is the sad feeling when hopes are not met, close to regret.

clue.text: Improvised trip inspired by New York-style jazz music of the 1990s

indicators.note: improvised means made up on the spot, so the letters are freely rearranged
to be inspired is literally to be breathed in, so one piece is taken inside another

blocks.note: bop, or bebop, is a jazz style developed in New York
taken as written

explanation.surface: An improvised trip influenced by jazz, described as the music of a decade.
explanation.walkthrough: Bebop grew up in New York clubs in the 1940s, hence 'New York-style'. The rearranged four letters sit inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Britpop was the wave of British guitar bands such as Oasis and Blur that peaked in the mid-1990s.

clue.text: Hold up a shopping centre, being from South America?

indicators.note: in a down clue, holding something up lifts it so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
a mall is a shopping centre

explanation.surface: An armed robbery at a shopping centre by someone from South America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold up' reads as a robbery; in a down clue it lifts the letters. 'Being' is a noun, a living creature, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The llama is an animal native to the Andes, so it is a creature originating in South America.

clue.text: What optician flogs on radio spots

indicators.note: radio is heard, not seen, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: specs is short for spectacles, which opticians sell

explanation.surface: An optician advertises in radio slots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spots' looks like advertising slots on the radio; it is the definition. To flog is British slang for to sell.
explanation.definitionFit: Specks are tiny marks or particles, the same as small spots.

clue.text: Two articles about bad-tempered management everywhere

indicators.note: about means around, so the outer pieces go round an inner one

blocks.note: the indefinite and definite articles
cross means irritable
a company's board of directors manages it

explanation.surface: Two newspaper articles about grumpy bosses appear in every paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' suggests newspaper pieces; it means the grammatical words, which surround the bad-tempered word before the management follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Across the board is an idiom for applying to all cases or areas without exception.

clue.text: Dawn’s twisted jokes going round university

indicators.note: twisted round means turned about, so the letters run backwards
going round something encircles it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: puns are jokes on words
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A woman called Dawn tells warped jokes around the campus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dawn's' looks like a woman's name with a possessive; it is the definition followed by 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunup is an informal word for sunrise, the time at the start of the day.

clue.text: Actors exit after the writer offers rebuke

indicators.note: coming after means following behind, so the piece named first in the clue is placed second

blocks.note: the cast is the set of actors in a production
the writer of the clue refers to himself as I
a gate is a way out

explanation.surface: The actors walk out after the playwright scolds them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The writer' is the setter, giving I. 'After' places the exit behind that letter, while the actors lead.
explanation.definitionFit: To castigate is to reprimand someone severely, a stronger synonym for scolding.

clue.text: Rub flanks of animal, old beast of burden

indicators.note: flanks are the sides, so only the outermost letters are wanted

blocks.note: to buff is to polish by rubbing
the two end letters of the word
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Someone rubs the sides of an elderly working animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flanks' suggests stroking an animal's sides; here it picks out the end letters of the word itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Water buffalo are widely used to pull ploughs and carts, making them working draught animals.

clue.text: Deviant leapt to interrupt vacuous punk rallying cry

indicators.note: deviant means straying from the norm, so the letters leave their usual order
vacuous means empty, so the inside is removed and only the ends stay
interrupting breaks into the middle of something, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: the word with its middle emptied out
taken as written

explanation.surface: A deviant jumps in to disrupt an empty-headed punk's battle cry.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged five letters sit between the outer letters of the punk. The definition is loose: a rousing speech rather than a single shout.
explanation.definitionFit: A pep talk is a short encouraging speech meant to rouse a team, much like a call to rally.

clue.text: Checking out without paying?

blocks.note: surface reading: leaving a hotel or shop till without settling the bill
setter's reading: looking over goods in displays with no intention of buying

explanation.walkthrough: 'Checking out' suggests leaving a hotel or passing a till, so the clue sounds like theft; it actually means having a look.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes browsing goods displayed in shop fronts without making any purchase.

clue.text: Son maybe injured fox in Kent

indicators.note: something injured is damaged out of shape, so the letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A son has perhaps hurt a fox in the English county of Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' marks the son as one example; the answer covers any closest relative.
explanation.definitionFit: A son is an example of a closest living relative, the person usually named as one's legal next of kin.

clue.text: Rose, seeing that Conservative, ran out

blocks.note: as in the sense of because or since
C is the abbreviation for Conservative
something that ran out came to an end

explanation.surface: A woman named Rose, noticing a Tory politician, fled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' at the start takes a capital and looks like a name; it is the past tense of rise.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose and ascended are both past tenses of verbs meaning went upward.

clue.text: People rarely call in these places now

definitions.text: People rarely call in these places now

blocks.clueFragment: People rarely call in these places now
blocks.note: surface reading: shops or houses people seldom drop in to visit these days

blocks.clueFragment: People rarely call in these places now
blocks.note: setter's reading: kiosks from which hardly anyone makes a phone call since mobiles took over

explanation.walkthrough: 'Call in' usually means pay a visit; here it means making a phone call from inside. Britain's red kiosks are now largely unused.
explanation.definitionFit: Public call kiosks on streets have become rarely used since mobile phones became universal.

clue.text: Permit partly misspelt – it never gets raised

indicators.note: partly means in part, so only a portion of the run of letters is used
in a down clue, raising something makes it read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the last three letters of the first word, the whole second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A complaint that a misspelt permit never gets approved.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run upward through the words, so they are found written backwards in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To entitle someone to something is to give them the right to it, or allow it.

clue.text: Howl over web item increasing gun danger?

blocks.note: hounds bay, a long howling bark
O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for over
a net is a web of mesh

explanation.surface: Outrage online at an internet post that raises the risk of shootings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Web item' looks like an online post; 'web' belongs to the wordplay and 'item' begins the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A blade fixed to a rifle muzzle adds stabbing to shooting, making the weapon more dangerous.

clue.text: Old rocker supporting Swedish group half-heartedly slowed down

indicators.note: with only half a heart, one of the two central letters is dropped
in a down clue a support holds from below, so the piece named first goes underneath the other

blocks.note: ABBA, the Swedish pop group, loses one of its middle letters
a Ted, or Teddy boy, was a 1950s British rock and roll fan

explanation.surface: An ageing rock star backing ABBA without enthusiasm eased off.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'supporting' puts one piece beneath another. A Teddy boy was a 1950s British youth in Edwardian-style dress who loved rock and roll.
explanation.definitionFit: Abated means lessened or eased in intensity, as a storm or pace slows down.

clue.text: Fly-by-night sort, husband yet to return – will it hold water?

indicators.note: to return is to come back, so the letters go back the way they came

blocks.note: bats fly at night
H is the abbreviation for husband
yet and but are both conjunctions of contrast

explanation.surface: A shady character's husband has not come back yet; will the story hold up?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly-by-night' normally means untrustworthy; read literally it is a creature flying at night. 'Hold water' usually means stand up to scrutiny.
explanation.definitionFit: A bath is a vessel built to be filled with water for washing in.

clue.text: Body part coming from revolutionary artificial intelligence section

indicators.note: a revolution turns things over, so the letters are turned round

blocks.note: AI is the standard abbreviation
a bit is a section or piece

explanation.surface: A body part produced by a groundbreaking AI department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like praise for the technology; it turns the whole five-letter string round.
explanation.definitionFit: The tibia is the shinbone, the larger of the two bones of the lower leg.

clue.text: Could European stick with dancing?

blocks.note: may and could both express possibility
a Pole is a person from Poland

explanation.surface: Asking whether a European might keep up with dance lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick with' reads as persevere; it is a noun phrase, a tall stick associated with dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: A maypole is a tall decorated post that people dance around on May Day in English folk tradition.

clue.text: In which urbanite travels, saving time?

definitions.text: In which urbanite travels, saving time?

indicators.note: saving means keeping safe within, so one letter is held inside
travel moves things about, so the letters change places

blocks.note: taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A city dweller commutes by a quick way, cutting journey time.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer, while the same words scramble a city dweller plus T. The Tube is London's underground railway.
explanation.definitionFit: A city resident rides an underground train as a faster way to cross town than by road.

clue.text: Exposed college official over framing king

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, so the letters run backwards
a frame surrounds a picture, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: a dean is a senior university or college administrator
K is the chess notation for king

explanation.surface: A university administrator is revealed to have set up a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Framing' suggests falsely incriminating someone; here it means placing around.
explanation.definitionFit: Naked and exposed both mean uncovered, laid bare to view.

clue.text: There’s only one way to depart from these exact conclusions

definitions.text: There’s only one way to depart from these

blocks.note: dead means exact, as in dead centre
ends are conclusions

explanation.surface: A remark that from these precise conclusions there is only one way out.
explanation.walkthrough: The long first half is a cryptic definition: from a road with no exit you can only leave the way you came.
explanation.definitionFit: A cul-de-sac or blind alley has no through route, so you must go back out the way you entered.

clue.text: Street in Rome, I start to drive out of it

indicators.note: the start is the beginning, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: St is the abbreviation for street
I is the Roman numeral for one
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A tourist on a Roman street begins to drive away from it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Street in Rome' tempts you towards VIA; the city only signals that I is a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Being out of it is slang for being intoxicated, especially high on drugs.
